purpose: Define the complete, compilable shape and exact observable behavior of monokl's query language -- query/mod.rs's public re-exports, query/lexer.rs's Token enum and Lexer, query/parser.rs's Modifier enum, ParsedTerm struct, parse() function and content_to_term() helper, and query/plan.rs's QueryPlan struct -- per docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Section 5 (lines 643-897), so a developer implementing or testing the query pipeline never has to guess a token boundary, an escape rule, a modifier's fate through a specific input, or which terms search_patterns() actually surfaces. Unlike every prior track this project has spec'd, this cluster is dominated by algorithmic behavior, not type shape: Lexer.next_token()'s dispatch rules, read_quoted()'s escape handling, and parse()'s multi-token lookahead logic each admit precise, non-obvious, and in one case (the "+regex:foo" input) already-documented failure behavior that only a careful trace of the actual control flow reveals. This track traces that control flow exactly, including docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md finding #8's precise claim -- that "+regex:foo" doesn't merely lose its Required modifier as the code's own comment states, but discards the regex semantics entirely, degrading to an Optional, escaped-literal match on the bare word "foo" -- by tracing parser.rs's exact token-by-token handling of that input, not by restating the finding's own summary.
scope: query/mod.rs's public re-export surface (Modifier, ParsedTerm, parse from parser; QueryPlan from plan); query/lexer.rs's Token enum (6 variants) and Lexer<'a> struct (2 private fields, zero derives, 2 public methods, 6 private helper methods); query/parser.rs's Modifier enum (3 variants), ParsedTerm struct (3 fields), the parse() function's complete token-dispatch logic including its LIMIT=64 term cap and empty-input early return, and the content_to_term() helper's exact Word/QuotedString/RegexPrefix/other handling; and query/plan.rs's QueryPlan struct (4 fields) and its from_terms/is_empty/search_patterns methods -- all verbatim per 01-core-architecture.md:643-897. It locks: Token's structural shape and Lexer's total lack of any derive; the exact dispatch order and byte-consumption behavior of Lexer::next_token() for each of Plus/Minus/quote/regex-prefix/word/Eof; read_word()'s greedy-until-whitespace consumption (so '+'/'-'/'"' are only special at token-start, never mid-word); read_quoted()'s single-escape (\") rule and its silent tolerance of an unterminated quoted string; the precise, traced consequence of "+regex:foo" and bare "regex:" inputs, including cases where a regex: prefix produces zero terms; parse()'s term-count cap and its exact interaction with the already-locked MonoklError::TooManyTerms variant (SPEC-001 AC-008); that regex pattern validity is never checked at this layer; and QueryPlan's exact term-to-category partitioning and search_patterns()'s required-then-scored (never excluded) output ordering.
non_goals: tokens.rs's tokenize()/tokenize_source() functions (docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Section 6) -- a separate, later track (Track 7 per .claude/plans/ACTIVE.md).

text_search.rs's search_files() and the rank/ module's consumption of QueryPlan and its search_patterns() output (docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Sections 7-8) -- separate, later tracks (Tracks 8-9).

MonoklError's own enum shape, Display text, or any variant other than confirming TooManyTerms's already-locked construction site here -- already locked by SPEC-001; this track states only that parse() constructs MonoklError::TooManyTerms { count: terms.len(), limit: 64 } at one specific point, per SPEC-001 AC-008's existing Display-text lock.

Whether an is_regex: true term's pattern string is ever validated as a syntactically valid regex, and the specific, already-documented inconsistency between two later pipeline stages' handling of an invalid one (docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #7, cited as context) -- this track states only that parser.rs itself performs no such validation; resolving or even fully describing finding #7's downstream inconsistency is a later track's responsibility.

Whether QueryPlan's is_empty() should instead check required/scored specifically rather than total term count, or whether an exclusion-only query (docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #21, cited as context) should surface a diagnostic -- this track documents QueryPlan's current, verbatim is_empty() semantics precisely; deciding whether to change them is a behavioral decision for whichever track implements the search command's own query-plan consumption.

api_surface.name: Lexer::new
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:673-675. Constructs a Lexer positioned at the start of input (pos: 0). Never fails.

api_surface.name: Lexer::next_token
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:736-752. Advances the lexer past leading whitespace, then returns exactly one Token, mutating the lexer's internal position. Never returns a Result; malformed input (e.g. an unterminated quoted string) produces a Token, never an error. See AC-004 through AC-007.

api_surface.name: parse
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:778-837. Tokenizes and interprets the full input string into a Vec<ParsedTerm>, applying the modifier/regex-prefix/term-count-limit logic in AC-009 through AC-015. Returns Ok(Vec::new()) for whitespace-only input, Err(MonoklError::TooManyTerms) if more than 64 terms result, Ok(terms) otherwise -- never any other error variant.
error_conditions: MonoklError::TooManyTerms { count, limit: 64 } when the parsed term count exceeds 64 (SPEC-001 AC-008).

api_surface.name: QueryPlan::from_terms
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:873-884. Partitions terms by modifier into required/excluded/scored index vectors, each preserving the relative order of the matching terms' original positions in terms. Never fails; an empty terms vec produces a QueryPlan with all four fields empty.

api_surface.name: QueryPlan::is_empty
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:886. Returns self.terms.is_empty() -- true only when the total term count (across all three categories combined) is zero. See AC-018 for the consequence on exclusion-only queries.

api_surface.name: QueryPlan::search_patterns
api_surface.description: 01-core-architecture.md:888-892. Returns pattern strings for required-category terms first, then scored-category terms, each in its own preserved relative order; excluded-category terms never appear in this method's output. See AC-019.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Token (01-core-architecture.md:657-665) compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] -- no Eq, no Copy, no Serialize/Deserialize -- and exactly 6 variants in this order: Plus (unit), Minus (unit), RegexPrefix (unit), QuotedString(String) (1-tuple), Word(String) (1-tuple), Eof (unit). Token has no JSON representation whatsoever: it never appears in any serde-derived struct's field, and attempting to use it where Serialize/Deserialize is required would be a compile-time E0277 failure naming Token specifically, the same class of consequence SPEC-006 AC-015 and SPEC-008 AC-002 establish for LineHit and TsconfigMode.

Lexer<'a> (01-core-architecture.md:667-670) carries NO derive attribute of any kind -- not Debug, not Clone, not PartialEq, nothing -- making it the first type this project has locked with zero derives at all; every other type with a reduced derive set (LineHit, TsconfigMode, WorkspaceOptions) still carries at least #[derive(Debug, Clone)]. Its 2 fields, input: &'a str and pos: usize, are both private (no pub keyword on either), so no code outside query/lexer.rs's own impl block can read or construct a Lexer's fields directly -- the only way to obtain one is Lexer::new.

Lexer's public API surface is exactly the 2 methods listed in api_surface -- new and next_token. The 6 other methods defined in its impl block (remaining, peek, advance, skip_whitespace, read_word, read_quoted; 01-core-architecture.md:677-734) are all private (no pub keyword), and are implementation details of next_token's own logic, not part of Lexer's public contract -- a caller outside query/lexer.rs cannot call any of them directly, and their exact behavior is described here (AC-005, AC-006) only insofar as it determines next_token's own observable output, not as an independently-callable contract.

Lexer::next_token() (01-core-architecture.md:736-752) always calls skip_whitespace() first, unconditionally consuming every leading ASCII-whitespace byte before inspecting the next character. It then dispatches on the first non-whitespace character in this exact order: no character remaining (EOF) produces Token::Eof; '+' consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Plus, regardless of what character (if any) follows; '-' likewise consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Minus; '"' consumes exactly 1 byte (the opening quote) and then delegates to read_quoted() to produce Token::QuotedString(...) (AC-006); any other character first checks whether the remaining input starts with the exact, case-sensitive 6-byte literal "regex:" -- if so, consumes exactly those 6 bytes and produces Token::RegexPrefix, with no lookahead at what follows; otherwise, delegates to read_word() to produce Token::Word(...) (AC-005). This dispatch order means '+', '-', and '"' are checked before the "regex:" prefix check, which is in turn checked before falling back to a generic word.

read_word() (01-core-architecture.md:701-714) greedily consumes every character from the current position up to (but not including) the next ASCII-whitespace character or EOF, with no other stopping condition -- '+', '-', '"', and the literal substring "regex:" are ordinary characters to read_word and do not terminate it early when they occur anywhere other than the very first character of a token (which next_token's own dispatch, AC-004, has already special-cased before read_word is ever called). Consequence: the input "foo+bar" tokenizes as a single Token::Word("foo+bar") -- the '+' does not split it into separate Plus and Word tokens, because next_token only inspects the FIRST character of a token to decide dispatch, and read_word does not stop at internal '+' characters once it has been invoked.

read_quoted() (01-core-architecture.md:716-734) is called after next_token has already consumed the opening '"'; it repeatedly calls advance() (which consumes and returns the next character) and, on each iteration: a closing '"' or EOF (None) ends the loop, with the closing quote itself (if present) consumed but not appended to the result string, and with NO error raised in either case -- an unterminated quoted string (EOF reached before any closing '"') returns whatever characters were accumulated so far as a normal, successful QuotedString value, indistinguishable from a properly-terminated one by its return type alone. A backslash character triggers a peek (not a consuming advance) at the next character: if that peeked character is exactly '"', the closing-quote lookalike is consumed (an additional pos += 1) and a single literal '"' is appended to the result -- this is the ONLY recognized escape sequence. For any other peeked character (including another backslash, or no character at all if input ends immediately after the initial backslash), the backslash itself is appended literally to the result and the peeked character (if any) is left unconsumed, to be processed as an ordinary character on read_quoted's next loop iteration. Any character other than a closing quote or a backslash is appended to the result as-is. Concrete examples below describe each input as an explicit sequence of characters, spelling out any backslash or quote character in words rather than relying on a backtick-quoted code span to convey a precise character count, since a code span cannot by itself distinguish "one backslash character" from "a source-level escape sequence representing one backslash character" -- the same ambiguity that made an earlier draft of this criterion self-contradictory. Example 1: input is the 5 characters quote, f, o, o, quote (no backslashes) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: f, o, o. Example 2: input is the 6 characters quote, a, backslash, quote, b, quote (a backslash immediately followed by a quote character) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: a, quote, b -- the escaped quote is appended literally and does NOT terminate the string. Example 3: input is the 6 characters quote, a, backslash, backslash, b, quote (a backslash immediately followed by ANOTHER backslash character) -> Token::QuotedString with a 4-character payload: a, backslash, backslash, b -- containing two literal backslash characters, not one: the first backslash peeks at the second, sees it is not a quote, appends the first backslash literally and leaves the second backslash unconsumed; the next loop iteration then advances past that second backslash, which itself peeks at the following 'b', sees it is not a quote, and appends the second backslash literally too -- neither backslash is treated as an escape, and neither is dropped. Example 4: input is the 3 characters quote, a, backslash, with NO closing quote at all (EOF immediately follows the backslash) -> Token::QuotedString with a 2-character payload: a, backslash -- containing a trailing literal backslash: advance() consumes the backslash, peek() returns None (not a quote), so the wildcard arm appends the backslash literally; the next loop iteration's advance() returns None (EOF), ending the loop with no error -- this is simultaneously an unterminated-string case and a trailing-escape case, and both tolerances compose silently.

Because Token::Plus and Token::Minus each consume exactly 1 byte with no lookahead (AC-004), and because query/parser.rs's parse() function (AC-010) calls lexer.next_token() a second, independent time to obtain the modifier's associated content -- which itself begins with skip_whitespace() (AC-004) -- the presence or absence of whitespace between a '+'/'-' and its following term has no effect on the resulting ParsedTerm: the inputs "+foo" and "+ foo" both tokenize as [Token::Plus, Token::Word("foo")] and both parse to the identical single Required ParsedTerm with pattern "foo". The identical whitespace-insensitivity holds for Minus: because Token::Minus also consumes exactly 1 byte with no lookahead (AC-004), and parse()'s Minus arm also calls lexer.next_token() a second, independent time (beginning with skip_whitespace()) to obtain the modifier's content, the inputs "-foo" and "- foo" both tokenize as [Token::Minus, Token::Word("foo")] and both parse to the identical single Excluded ParsedTerm with pattern "foo".

Modifier (01-core-architecture.md:764-769) compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)] and exactly 3 variants in this order: Required, Excluded, Optional -- all unit variants, no serde derive. ParsedTerm (01-core-architecture.md:771-776) compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone)] only -- no PartialEq, no Eq, no serde derive -- and exactly 3 fields in this order: modifier: Modifier, pattern: String, is_regex: bool. Neither type has any JSON representation; both are internal parsing primitives, the same zero-serde-contract class AC-001 establishes for Token. All 3 fields are declared pub. This is required, not incidental: query/plan.rs reads t.modifier (01-core-architecture.md:875, 878, 881) and self.terms[i].pattern (01-core-architecture.md:890) across a module boundary from query/parser.rs, so declaring any of the three fields private is an E0616 compile failure naming that field.

parse() (01-core-architecture.md:778-837) begins with an early-return check, before constructing a Lexer at all: if input.trim().is_empty(), parse returns Ok(Vec::new()) immediately. This check uses Rust's default str::trim(), which trims by the Unicode White_Space derived property (matching char::is_whitespace()), NOT by ASCII whitespace alone -- it is true for an empty string, a string containing only ASCII whitespace (space, tab, newline, CR), AND a string containing only non-ASCII Unicode whitespace such as U+00A0 (NBSP), U+2003 (EM SPACE), or U+3000 (IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE). This is a distinct code path, checked before any Lexer exists, from the lexer ever tokenizing an empty or whitespace-only remainder -- and the two use DIFFERENT whitespace definitions: this early-return check uses str::trim()'s Unicode-whitespace rule against the FULL original (untrimmed) input string, while the Lexer's own skip_whitespace() (AC-004) uses ch.is_ascii_whitespace() exclusively and only ever operates on the original, untrimmed input passed to Lexer::new -- trim()'s result is never itself passed to the Lexer. Consequence for a non-ASCII-whitespace character: input consisting of a single U+00A0 (NBSP, e.g. "\u{00A0}") has input.trim().is_empty() == true (NBSP is Unicode whitespace), so parse("\u{00A0}") == Ok(Vec::new()) via this early-return path, without ever constructing a Lexer. By contrast, input "\u{00A0}foo" has input.trim().is_empty() == false (trim() strips the leading NBSP for the purposes of this check only, leaving non-empty "foo"), so the early-return does NOT fire; a Lexer is constructed over the ORIGINAL, untrimmed string "\u{00A0}foo", and its first next_token() call's skip_whitespace() does NOT skip the NBSP (is_ascii_whitespace() returns false for U+00A0), so peek() returns the NBSP character itself, which is not '+'/'-'/'"', does not start "regex:", and falls to read_word() -- which greedily consumes the NBSP as an ordinary character (it is not ASCII whitespace) along with "foo", producing exactly one Token::Word("\u{00A0}foo") containing the leading NBSP as part of the word's text, which content_to_term()/AC-012 then turns into a single Optional ParsedTerm with pattern regex::escape("\u{00A0}foo") == "\u{00A0}foo" (NBSP is not a regex metacharacter).

For each Token::Plus or Token::Minus encountered in parse()'s main loop (01-core-architecture.md:789-800), the very next lexer.next_token() call's result ("content") is passed to content_to_term(content, modifier), where modifier is Modifier::Required for Plus and Modifier::Excluded for Minus. content_to_term (01-core-architecture.md:839-854) produces Some(ParsedTerm { modifier, pattern: regex::escape(&w_or_s), is_regex: false }) when content is Token::Word(w) or Token::QuotedString(s) -- using the modifier passed in, not Modifier::Optional -- and produces None (pushing no term at all for that Plus/Minus occurrence) for every other content value, including Token::RegexPrefix (with an explicit source comment: "`+regex:foo` documented as silently losing modifier") and any of Token::Plus/Token::Minus/Token::Eof as the content.

For each bare Token::RegexPrefix encountered directly in parse()'s main loop (01-core-architecture.md:801-813, i.e. not consumed as another token's "content" per AC-010), the next lexer.next_token() call's result ("pattern_tok") is matched: Token::Word(raw) or Token::QuotedString(raw) produces a ParsedTerm { modifier: Modifier::Optional, pattern: raw, is_regex: true } -- using the RAW token content directly, with no regex::escape() applied, unlike every other term-producing arm in parse(). Any other pattern_tok value (Token::Eof, Token::Plus, Token::Minus, or another Token::RegexPrefix) matches the wildcard arm and produces no term at all for that RegexPrefix occurrence -- a bare "regex:" at the very end of the input, or immediately followed by another "+"/"-"/"regex:", silently contributes zero terms to the result, with no error raised. Concrete trace for the non-Eof wildcard cases: for input "regex: -foo", the exact sequence is: next_token() produces Token::RegexPrefix (consuming the 6-byte "regex:" literal); parse()'s RegexPrefix arm then calls lexer.next_token() for pattern_tok, which -- after skip_whitespace() consumes the single space -- dispatches on '-' and produces Token::Minus, PERMANENTLY consuming that '-' byte off the lexer; pattern_tok = Token::Minus matches the wildcard arm, so no term is pushed for the RegexPrefix occurrence AND the Minus token itself is never processed as its own Excluded-modifier occurrence -- it is not rewound or reprocessed, it is simply gone. Control returns to parse()'s main loop, which calls lexer.next_token() again; the lexer's position now sits at the unconsumed "foo" with no leading whitespace, producing Token::Word("foo") fresh, which (per AC-012) produces a single Optional, non-regex ParsedTerm with pattern "foo". The net, fully-traced result for "regex: -foo" is exactly one ParsedTerm: an Optional match on "foo" -- the Excluded/Minus modifier that immediately followed "regex:" is discarded entirely, with no diagnostic, the same swallowed-lookahead-token pattern AC-013 documents for "+regex:foo". For input "regex:" alone (bare prefix at end of input, the other wildcard case), pattern_tok = Token::Eof (nothing left to consume), matches the wildcard arm, no term is pushed, and the main loop's next lexer.next_token() call also returns Token::Eof, ending the loop -- parse("regex:") == Ok(Vec::new()).

A Token::Word(w) or Token::QuotedString(s) encountered directly in parse()'s main loop, not preceded by a Plus/Minus/RegexPrefix (01-core-architecture.md:814-827), each produce a ParsedTerm { modifier: Modifier::Optional, pattern: regex::escape(&w_or_s), is_regex: false } -- both token variants receive identical treatment (Optional modifier, escaped pattern, is_regex: false) despite one representing an unquoted word and the other a quoted string; the only observable difference between the two is which characters the original input's word-boundary and quote-escaping rules (AC-005, AC-006) allowed into the token's own String payload before this point.

For the specific input "+regex:foo", the exact traced sequence is: Token::Plus is produced first (consuming the leading '+', AC-004); parse()'s Plus arm then calls lexer.next_token() for "content", which -- since the lexer's position now sits at "regex:foo" with no leading whitespace -- matches the "regex:" prefix check (AC-004) and consumes exactly "regex:" (6 bytes), producing Token::RegexPrefix as the content value, WITHOUT consuming "foo"; content_to_term(Token::RegexPrefix, Modifier::Required) then returns None per AC-010, so nothing is pushed for the "+regex:" portion -- both the Required modifier AND the regex intent are discarded at this point, not merely the modifier. Control then returns to parse()'s main loop, which calls lexer.next_token() again; since the lexer's position now sits at the unconsumed "foo" with no leading whitespace, this produces Token::Word("foo") fresh, which -- per AC-012, not AC-010 or AC-011 -- produces a ParsedTerm { modifier: Modifier::Optional, pattern: regex::escape("foo"), is_regex: false }. The net, fully-traced result for "+regex:foo" is exactly one ParsedTerm: an Optional, non-regex, escaped-literal match on "foo" -- matching docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #8's exact characterization: "tracing the lexer shows it actually degrades all the way to an optional escaped-literal match on the string `foo` — both the required-modifier *and* the regex semantics are discarded, not just the modifier." Because parse()'s Minus arm (01-core-architecture.md:795-800) calls content_to_term(content, Modifier::Excluded) via the identical structure as the Plus arm -- same lookahead call, same content_to_term function, differing only in the Modifier value passed -- the input "-regex:foo" degrades through the identical traced sequence: Token::Minus is produced first; the Minus arm's lexer.next_token() lookahead matches the "regex:" prefix and produces Token::RegexPrefix as content, WITHOUT consuming "foo"; content_to_term(Token::RegexPrefix, Modifier::Excluded) returns None per AC-010, discarding both the Excluded modifier and the regex intent; the main loop's next lexer.next_token() call then produces Token::Word("foo") fresh, which (per AC-012) yields a single Optional, non-regex ParsedTerm with pattern "foo" -- the net result for "-regex:foo" is identical in kind to "+regex:foo": an Optional, escaped-literal match on "foo", with the Excluded modifier silently discarded, not merely weakened.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: This criterion states the exact, hand-traced control-flow consequence for one specific input, matching an already-documented finding, rather than a general structural fact -- included because the finding's own text explicitly contrasts this behavior against a weaker claim ("the code comment says it 'silently loses modifier'"), so precisely which of the two characterizations is correct is itself the testable content here, not merely a restatement.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: parse() checks terms.len() > LIMIT (where LIMIT: usize = 64 is a local const, 01-core-architecture.md:779) only AFTER its main token-consuming loop has fully completed (01-core-architecture.md:830-835) -- every term in the input is parsed into the terms Vec regardless of how many there are, and only once parsing is entirely finished does the length check run. Exactly 64 terms succeeds (the check is strictly greater-than, not greater-than-or-equal); 65 or more terms fails with Err(MonoklError::TooManyTerms { count: terms.len(), limit: 64 }), constructing the variant SPEC-001 AC-008 already locks the exact shape and Display text for ("query has too many terms: {count} > {limit}") -- this track does not re-lock TooManyTerms's own shape, only that parse() constructs it at this specific point with these specific field values.

No code in query/parser.rs attempts to compile, validate, or otherwise check the syntactic validity of an is_regex: true term's pattern string -- the raw token content from a "regex:" prefix (AC-011) is stored directly into ParsedTerm.pattern with no processing beyond the token-extraction itself. A syntactically invalid regex pattern (e.g. an unbalanced parenthesis, "regex:(unclosed") parses successfully at this layer, producing a ParsedTerm with is_regex: true and pattern: "(unclosed" exactly as given, with no error raised by parse() itself. Whether and when this pattern is later rejected (or silently ignored) is a downstream, later-pipeline-stage concern -- docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #7 documents that two later stages handle an invalid pattern inconsistently (one hard-fails the whole query, the other silently drops the failing term) -- this track does not resolve or restate that inconsistency beyond noting that parser.rs's own contribution to it is performing no validation at all.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: Citing finding #7 as context for why parser.rs's total absence of validation matters requires care not to claim this track resolves or fully describes the downstream inconsistency, which is explicitly out of scope per non_goals.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: QueryPlan (01-core-architecture.md:864-870) compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone)] only -- no serde derive -- and exactly 4 fields in this order: terms: Vec<ParsedTerm>, required: Vec<usize>, excluded: Vec<usize>, scored: Vec<usize>. All 4 fields are declared pub, so a QueryPlan can be constructed by struct literal from any module, not only via from_terms -- a fact AC-019 depends on.

QueryPlan::from_terms (01-core-architecture.md:873-884) builds required, excluded, and scored by independently iterating terms.iter().enumerate() three times, each time filtering on a distinct Modifier variant (Required, Excluded, Optional respectively) and collecting the matching indices via .map(|(i, _)| i) -- with no re-sorting applied to any of the three resulting Vec<usize>, so each preserves the relative order its matching terms had in the original terms Vec. Because Modifier has exactly 3 variants and every ParsedTerm carries exactly one Modifier value, every index 0..terms.len() appears in exactly one of required/excluded/scored, never zero and never more than one.

QueryPlan::is_empty() (01-core-architecture.md:886) returns self.terms.is_empty() -- the total term count across all three categories combined, not whether required or scored (the two categories search_patterns() actually returns, per AC-019) are individually non-empty. Consequence: a QueryPlan built entirely from excluded terms (e.g. from an exclusion-only query like "-foo -bar", with zero Required or Optional terms) reports is_empty() == false, even though search_patterns() would return an empty Vec<&str> for that same QueryPlan -- docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #21 documents that exclusion-only queries "always silently return an empty response with no diagnostic explaining that this is a no-op by design," a downstream consequence this track does not resolve (see non_goals) but which is directly connected to is_empty()'s specific definition locked here.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: Connecting is_empty()'s exact semantics to finding #21's downstream symptom required care to state the connection (a QueryPlan can report non-empty while having nothing for search_patterns() to return) without claiming this track resolves or even fully explains why the downstream no-op produces no diagnostic, which is out of scope per non_goals.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: QueryPlan::search_patterns() (01-core-architecture.md:888-892) returns self.required.iter().chain(self.scored.iter()).map(|&i| self.terms[i].pattern.as_str()).collect() -- required-category pattern strings first, in required's own preserved order (AC-017), followed by scored-category pattern strings in scored's own preserved order; excluded-category terms are not chained in at all, so for any QueryPlan produced by QueryPlan::from_terms (AC-017), excluded-category terms never appear in this method's return value. This guarantee holds only for from_terms-built plans: because QueryPlan's four fields are all pub (AC-016), a QueryPlan can also be constructed directly by struct literal with required/excluded/scored index vectors that do not correspond to any from_terms partition of terms, and in that case an excluded-looking term's pattern can appear in search_patterns()'s output if its index is placed in required or scored directly. This ordering is by category, not by each term's original position in the input: for an input parsing to terms [scored_term_at_idx_0, required_term_at_idx_1] (a scored term appearing before a required term in the raw query text), required = [1] and scored = [0], so search_patterns() returns [terms[1].pattern, terms[0].pattern] -- the required term's pattern first, despite having appeared second in the original input.

Lexer::next_token() and its helpers operate correctly on multi-byte UTF-8 input without panicking or truncating a character, because self.pos is advanced by a consumed char's own ch.len_utf8() in advance(), skip_whitespace(), and read_word(); by "regex:".len() (a hardcoded 6) immediately after starts_with("regex:") has verified the prefix is present; and by a literal 1 at exactly four other sites -- next_token()'s '+', '-', and '"' dispatch arms (each firing only after peek() has confirmed the byte at pos is that exact single-byte ASCII character), and read_quoted()'s escaped-quote arm (self.pos += 1 immediately before pushing a literal '"', firing only after peek() has confirmed the next byte is an ASCII '"'). Every increment therefore lands on a UTF-8 char boundary, but not because all advancement is len_utf8()-based -- the four literal-1 sites are each guarded by a preceding peek()/match that has already proven the specific byte being skipped is a 1-byte ASCII character, which is what actually makes a literal +=1 safe at those four sites specifically. remaining()'s &self.input[self.pos..] slice never panics as a result. Concrete example: for input "+café" (é is the 2-byte UTF-8 sequence U+00E9), next_token() dispatches on '+' and produces Token::Plus (consuming exactly 1 byte); the modifier arm's next lexer.next_token() call skips no whitespace, sees 'c', does not match "regex:", and calls read_word(), which consumes c, a, f, and é as four distinct chars (é consumed as one char via chars().next(), advancing pos by its full 2-byte len_utf8(), not split across two 1-byte steps), producing Token::Word("café"); content_to_term(Word("café"), Required) yields ParsedTerm { modifier: Required, pattern: regex::escape("café"), is_regex: false } -- regex::escape leaves non-ASCII, non-metacharacter bytes unchanged, so pattern == "café" verbatim. So parse("+café") == Ok(vec![ParsedTerm { modifier: Required, pattern: "café".to_string(), is_regex: false }]). Equivalently, for a multi-byte character inside a quoted string, input "\"日本語\"" tokenizes via read_quoted() (each of 日/本/語 consumed as one char via advance(), none matching '"' or '\\', each appended as-is) to Token::QuotedString("日本語").
acceptance_criteria.rationale: No source document or prior finding calls out multi-byte-boundary safety explicitly -- this criterion states a structural correctness property (pos always sits on a char boundary) that follows not from exclusive len_utf8()-based advancement (four sites use a literal +=1 instead) but from each of those four literal-1 sites being individually guarded by a preceding peek()/match confirming the skipped byte is single-byte ASCII, worth locking given this track's purpose explicitly promises a developer never has to guess a token boundary, and non-ASCII input is a realistic case for a code-search tool indexing real source files.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: query/mod.rs (01-core-architecture.md:645-652) declares exactly 3 submodules, each as pub mod, in this order: pub mod lexer;, pub mod parser;, pub mod plan; -- none are private (bare mod) or path-attributed. It then declares exactly 2 pub use re-export lines, in this order: pub use parser::{Modifier, ParsedTerm, parse}; (a single grouped-brace re-export naming exactly these 3 items from the parser submodule, in this order) and pub use plan::QueryPlan; (a single-item re-export from the plan submodule). No other item from lexer, parser, or plan (e.g. Lexer, Token, or plan's own internal helpers) is re-exported at the mod.rs level -- a caller must reach Lexer and Token via query::lexer:: and has no query::Lexer or query::Token path available.

QueryPlan::search_patterns() indexes self.terms[i] for each i in required and scored (01-core-architecture.md:890) with no bounds check against terms.len(). Neither QueryPlan::from_terms nor any other code in query/plan.rs validates that an index vector's entries are all less than terms.len() before search_patterns() uses them -- from_terms itself always produces valid indices (AC-017), since it derives them directly from terms.iter().enumerate(), but because QueryPlan's fields are all pub (AC-016), a directly-constructed QueryPlan carrying an index in required, excluded, or scored that is greater than or equal to terms.len() causes search_patterns() to panic with an out-of-bounds index, not return an error or an empty result -- e.g. QueryPlan { terms: vec![], required: vec![5], excluded: vec![], scored: vec![] }.search_patterns() panics rather than returning Ok(vec![]) or Err(...). This panic path exists regardless of whether the QueryPlan was built via from_terms; the API surface gives search_patterns() no error_conditions because from_terms-built plans can never trigger it, but a directly-constructed one can.
acceptance_criteria.rationale: Surfacing an unchecked-index panic path that only a directly-constructed (not from_terms-built) QueryPlan can reach required distinguishing between "guaranteed-safe by from_terms's own construction" and "safe in general" -- the public struct's pub fields mean the invariant from_terms maintains is not enforced at the type level, so this is a real, reachable panic path worth locking precisely rather than assuming from_terms's own safety extends to every possible QueryPlan value.
